one_liner: C++ deterministic Wasm/EVM JIT for smart contracts. Its lazy JIT reaches first invocation about 20x sooner than Wasmtime's eager compile.
what_it_does: DTVM (engine code name ZetaEngine) is a blockchain VM that runs WebAssembly, and on current main also EVM bytecode, with deterministic semantics, gas metering and EVM ABI compatibility. It ships an interpreter, an asmjit-based singlepass JIT and an LLVM-15-based multipass JIT whose lazy mode compiles functions on demand. You embed it through C++ (src/zetaengine.h), a C API (src/zetaengine-c.h: ZenLoadModuleFromFile, host-module descriptors, ZenCallWasmFuncByIdx) or a Rust crate, or run the dtvm CLI. It is not a drop-in for the Wasmtime or Wasmer embedding APIs.
how_it_is_fast: Wasm and EVM are lowered to a deterministic middle IR (dMIR) and then to x86-64 code through an LLVM-derived backend. Lazy mode (FLAT, 'Function Level fAst Transpile') does only load, precompile, instantiation and the first called function's JIT before running. A background tier (FLAS, 'Function Level Adaptive hot-Switching') recompiles hot functions at higher optimisation levels and swaps them in through trampolines. Wasm traps and bounds checks use CPU exceptions (ZEN_ENABLE_CPU_EXCEPTION, on by default) instead of explicit checks. The startup win comes from deferring compilation, not from a faster compiler: the package's own docs put DTVM's eager multipass compile at about 90 ms on the current build, against about 20 ms for Wasmtime's whole-module compile.
when_to_use: Smart-contract or plugin hosts that load a module and call one or two exports, where time to first call matters more than peak throughput (the paper's TTFI case: about 0.95 ms vs about 20.5 ms for Wasmtime on PolyBench modules).

Systems that need deterministic execution, gas metering and checked integer arithmetic built into the JIT (ZEN_ENABLE_CHECKED_ARITHMETIC lowers imported checked_i64_* calls into inline checked operations).
Embedding a Wasm or EVM JIT from C or C++ with a small trusted computing base, including Intel SGX enclaves (ZEN_ENABLE_SGX).
Linux x86-64 deployments that can link LLVM 15 for the multipass/lazy JIT, or ARM64 hosts that can live with the singlepass JIT or interpreter.
when_not_to_use: Long-running compute: on PolyBench processing time it beats Wasmtime (Cranelift) in only 20 of 30 kernels (1.20x average where it wins, as slow as about 0.57x on trisolv), so steady-state code quality is roughly at par.

General-purpose WASI applications: the project is built for contracts. Builtin WASI and libc are partial ('builtin libc (partial)'), and support for proposals such as SIMD and threads is not documented in the README.
Non-x86-64 targets that need the optimising JIT: 'Lazy JIT currently only supports the x86-64 target'.
Multi-threaded embedding without your own locking: module and host-module APIs in zetaengine-c.h are marked '\warning not thread-safe'.
Teams wanting releases or semver: the GitHub Releases section is empty, and recent commit activity is almost all EVM-side work.

integration.form: static lib (libzetaengine.a) plus dtvm CLI; Rust crate in rust_crate/
integration.dependencies: LLVM 15 (multipass/lazy JIT only); asmjit, CLI11 and spdlog fetched via CMake FetchContent; evmc submodule for EVM builds
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 for multipass/lazy JIT; singlepass JIT on x86-64 and ARM64; interpreter portable; optional Intel SGX
integration.thread_safety: C API module load/delete and host-module functions are documented as not thread-safe; multipass JIT uses up to 8 compile threads by default and background JIT threads in lazy and profile-guided modes

gotchas: Harness flaw in the paper's Integer Overflow benchmark (5.5 ms, 20.6% less than Wasmtime): the runtimes run different programs. The DTVM wasm (-DENABLE_DTVM_TEST) imports env.checked_i64_add/sub/mul, which DTVM's module loader resolves and its bytecode visitor turns into inline checked arithmetic. The Wasmtime and Wasmer wasm uses __builtin_*_overflow, compiled to portable wasm, plus explicit divide-by-zero and INT64_MIN/-1 checks that the DTVM variant drops (it uses plain '/'). Wasmer also gets a third build with a main() entry. The gap therefore measures a DTVM-only intrinsic and less source-level work, not JIT quality, and the DTVM module cannot run on the other VMs. REPRODUCE_fib_overflow_5way.md calls this 'a real architectural advantage, not a testing artifact'.

The fib(30) figure (11.73 ms) is the shell `time` wall clock of one process running a recursive fib(30), so CLI startup and compilation dominate it. The package's current fib benchmark is a different workload (500,000,000 iterations of an 8x-unrolled iterative fib(30)), and its run_wasmtime45.sh omits the '-C cache=n' that the reproduction guide lists.

TTFI cannot be reproduced from public sources. The current paper pin c3c3fd856 (2026-05-29, '30% fib speedup') returns 404 on github.com. Main's src/utils/statistics.cpp, the file the package names, prints no 'Total compilation time' line, and the change note docs/changes/2026-05-28-wapm-ttfi-compile-time-report is absent. The Wasmtime 45 and Wasmer 7.1 timing patches are not shipped; only a Wasmtime 31 patch is. scripts/README.md calls the paper's DTVM formula 'inferred': load + precompile + instantiation + fg_jit/fg_count, an average per-function JIT time, measured against Wasmtime's whole compile_module().
The README build lines use CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, and the default CMake options leave the multipass JIT OFF. Benchmarking that build gives numbers far below the paper's Release build.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick DTVM over wasman (Go interpreter), WasmKit (Swift interpreter) or KinoWASM (interpreter) when you need an optimising x86-64 JIT with gas metering and determinism embedded from C/C++. Pick it over Cage when you want fast cold invocation rather than MTE memory safety. VectorVisor solves a different problem: batch GPU throughput.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own non-peer-reviewed preprint (Xeon Platinum 8369B cloud VM, CentOS 7.9, paper-era DTVM 882c83155 with LLVM 15, Wasmtime 31.0.0, Wasmer 5.0.x) reports about 22x faster time-to-first-invocation than Wasmtime (Cranelift) on 30 PolyBench modules. That compares a lazy compile of the first function against Wasmtime's eager whole-module compile. Whole-run processing time is mixed (20 of 30 PolyBench wins, 1.20x average there), and the fib and integer-overflow microbenchmarks are startup-dominated or compare different wasm programs.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-08, 157 stars, no tagged releases), now mostly on the EVM JIT. Apache-2.0 with LLVM-derived code, usable as a C/C++ library. Its performance evidence stays first-party, and the current reproduction pin, c3c3fd856, is not public.
